points: **Genetic predisposition** (e.g. HLA-C*06:02, linked with early-onset and guttate disease) plus immune activation.
Key cytokine axis: **IL-23 → Th17 → IL-17**, plus TNF-α, causing keratinocyte hyperproliferation and inflammation.
Very fast epidermal turnover produces thick, scaly plaques.
Streptococcal throat infection (guttate psoriasis)
Trauma, scratches and surgery: the **Koebner phenomenon**
Drugs: lithium, beta-blockers, antimalarials, and abrupt withdrawal of systemic steroids

points: **Well-demarcated**, deep red/shiny, **smooth** patches; scale often absent or minimal.
Fissure in crease depth common.
Sites: axillae, inframammary, groin, natal cleft, umbilicus, genitals, anus.
Check ears, scalp, elbows/knees, nails for supporting clues.
Complications: secondary yeast/bacteria, lichenification from itch (esp. perianal), sexual dysfunction/embarrassment, steroid atrophy from overuse.

items.name: Chronic plaque
items.t: Sharply demarcated red plaques with silvery-white scale; pinpoint bleeding when scale is removed (Auspitz sign)

items.name: Flexural (inverse)
items.t: Shiny, well-defined, moist, little or no scale; may be colonised by Candida
items.where: Axillae, groin, natal cleft, under the breasts

items.name: Guttate
items.t: Many small ‘raindrop’ plaques, often 2–3 weeks after a strep throat

items.name: Scalp
items.t: Thick adherent scale, often extending beyond the hairline

items.name: Nail
items.t: Pitting, onycholysis, oil-drop discolouration, subungual hyperkeratosis

points: morphology, distribution, nails and joints.
body surface area (BSA), high-impact sites (face, hands, genitals, scalp) and quality of life.
every year with the PEST questionnaire, especially in the first 10 years.
Biopsy if uncertain. Take a throat swab if guttate psoriasis follows a recent sore throat.

cards.name: Seborrhoeic dermatitis
cards.clue: Greasier scale on the central face; can overlap (‘sebopsoriasis’)

cards.name: Tinea corporis
cards.clue: Asymmetrical with an advancing edge; mycology positive

cards.name: Lichen planus
cards.clue: Violaceous, flat-topped papules with Wickham striae; wrists and mucosa

cards.name: Discoid eczema
cards.clue: Coin-shaped, very itchy, often on the legs

cards.name: Candidal intertrigo (vs flexural psoriasis)
cards.clue: Satellite papules and pustules, macerated; flexural psoriasis is sharply defined with no satellites

cards.name: Irritant intertrigo
cards.clue: Less sharply marginated; improves with dryness alone

cards.name: Seborrhoeic dermatitis
cards.clue: Ill-defined salmon-pink; greasy scalp/face involvement (“sebopsoriasis” overlap)

cards.name: Erythrasma
cards.clue: Brownish, quiet itch, Wood lamp coral-red

cards.name: Hailey–Hailey
cards.clue: Painful erosions/fissures, flaccid blisters, family history

points: Use emollients regularly. They reduce scale and itch and help active topicals work.
Lifestyle: weight loss if overweight, stopping smoking, moderating alcohol, and support with stress.
Seek review promptly for unexplained joint pain or swelling.
**Potent steroid once daily plus vitamin D analogue once daily**, applied at different times of day, for up to 4 weeks.
If not controlled: **vitamin D analogue twice daily** for 8–12 weeks.
Then either a potent steroid twice daily (short course) or coal tar, **or** fixed-combination **calcipotriol/betamethasone** once daily for up to 4 weeks, which helps adherence.
Plan a **4-week break** between courses of potent or very potent steroid, using a non-steroid topical in between.
Do not exceed the maximum durations: potent steroid **≤ 8 weeks** per site; very potent **≤ 4 weeks**, usually on specialist advice.

Methotrexate (often the first conventional option), ciclosporin (for rapid control or when planning conception) and acitretin, followed by biologics or TYK2 inhibitors under NICE technology appraisals.

items.t: **Erythroderma** (widespread redness over 90% of the skin) or **generalised pustular psoriasis**: same-day dermatology or hospital assessment.
Suspected **psoriatic arthritis** (swollen or painful joints, dactylitis, enthesitis): refer to rheumatology.
BSA over 10%, moderate or worse severity, failure of topicals, or a major impact on quality of life: refer for phototherapy or systemics.
Severe nail disease, children, and diagnostic uncertainty: refer.

pearls.t: Explain that psoriasis is **chronic** and treatment is intermittent. Most patients relapse after stopping.
Demonstrate how to apply treatment. Cosmetic acceptability drives adherence, so gels and foams often beat ointments for daytime use.
Spell out **steroid breaks** to prevent atrophy and rebound.
Calcipotriol/betamethasone combinations (Dovobet®-type gel, foam or ointment) vary by formulary, so check local brands.
**Avoid oral steroids.** Withdrawal can trigger rebound or pustular flares.
Counsel on vaccination and infection risk if the patient later moves to immunosuppression (specialist-led).
NICE notes a higher VTE risk in severe psoriasis, so keep it in mind.

Prescribing detail for vitamin D analogues, coal tar, dithranol and phototherapy: [vitamin D analogues, tar and phototherapy](condition:vitamin-d-tar-phototherapy); for patients on methotrexate or a biologic, see [biologics and systemics](condition:biologics-systemics).
